title: The clear and the doubtful
hookLine: the halal is clear, the haram is clear, between them are doubtful things, and in the body is a lump of flesh: the heart
tomorrow: the whole religion in one word. which word?

cards: On a cliff trail, the railing stands a few steps back from the drop. Nobody walking it complains that the fence comes too early. That's the whole idea of it.
Yesterday's question: between the allowed and the forbidden is a gray zone, so then what?
Al-Nu'man ibn Bashir reports the answer of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and it's built around a shepherd, a king's pasture, and, at the very end, the heart.

teach.h: CLEAR, CLEAR, AND A GRAY MIDDLE.
teach.b: The halal is clear, and the haram is clear, and between them are doubtful things that many people don't know. Whoever keeps clear of the doubtful protects their religion and their honor.

teach.h: A SHEPHERD AT THE KING'S PASTURE.
teach.b: Whoever slides into them is like a shepherd grazing along the edge of a king's private pasture: any moment, the flock is inside it. Every king has a pasture like that, and Allah's is what He has forbidden.
Then the hadith turns inward without warning. In the body there's a lump of flesh.
If it's sound, the whole body is sound; if it's corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. It is the heart. So the gray zone isn't finally about lists.
It's about what's steering. Here's ground Muslims share with a neighbor.

The Mishnah, in Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, opens with advice the sages handed down: make a fence around the Torah. Keep a margin, so you never come near the edge. The same railing, in Jewish words.
And one honest difference. In Jewish law, the sages built such fences as shared rulings for a whole community to keep.
In this hadith, stepping back from the doubtful is left to each person's caution, and the hadith ends there, on the heart.

how: When Muslims meet something whose ruling is unclear, such as a food without a clear label, they are encouraged to keep clear of it until they know, or to ask someone with knowledge.

games.q: what does “the clear and the doubtful” mean?
o: a list of the foods that are allowed and forbidden
the difference between big sins and little ones
the plain allowed, the plain forbidden, and a gray middle

games.q: the clear, the doubtful, the heart — tap the pairs.
p: grazing at the edge of the pasture
make a fence around the Torah

s: if something isn't clearly forbidden, it's automatically fine
the hadith names a doubtful middle, and says keeping clear of it protects your religion and your honor.
the hadith ends on the heart, not on a list of rules
in the body is a lump of flesh: if it's sound, the whole body is sound. it is the heart.
the doubtful things are just the forbidden ones under another name
the hadith keeps three zones: clear, clear, and a doubtful middle that many people don't know.

games.q: a new energy drink is everywhere at school. the label lists an ingredient you can't identify, and you can't find out if it's halal. what fits the hadith?
o: skip it for now; keeping clear of the doubtful protects your religion.
drink it: if it isn't clearly haram, then it must be halal.
tell everyone it's haram, since anything doubtful is forbidden.
games.why: the hadith keeps the doubtful as its own zone: not declared haram, but worth stepping back from, like a railing before the drop.

practice: Rest a hand over your heart and close your eyes. Bring to mind one gray thing from your week, something you're honestly not sure about.
Don't argue it either way; just notice which way your heart leans, and if it's doubtful, let today be the day you step back from it.

wordCard.voice: The clear and the doubtful: halal clear, haram clear, and a gray middle between them. The guard on that middle is the heart.

orig.note: Arabic: the halal is clear, the hadith's opening words.

carryVoice: To keep: guard the heart, and the gray zone gets easier to walk. Eight days into year five.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 52; Sahih Muslim 1599 (al-Nu'man ibn Bashir: the halal is clear, the haram is clear; the shepherd and the sanctuary; the heart)
Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 1:1 (make a fence around the Torah)
